comment: The §4.1c mutation ledger. Each entry is a CONCRETE PATCH -- a file, an anchor that must
occur exactly once, and its replacement -- never a sentence describing an edit. A sentence
cannot be replayed; a patch can, and `npm run test:mutation` replays every one of these on
every run.
A KILL IS DEFINED BY FOUR RULES, and scripts/mutate.mjs enforces all four:
1. the owning test PASSED unmutated, in the same run;
2. the patch actually CHANGED the file (anchor unique, bytes different, and the reverse
patch restores the original md5);
3. the run served the MUTATED code -- proved two ways, because one is not enough: the
built bundle's hash must MOVE, and the failure must not match a shape that means the
code never ran at all (a build error, a server that never started, a refused
connection);
4. the failure is the NAMED TEST's own assertion, not the suite going red for some other
reason.
A patch that does not compile is DOES NOT BUILD and is never a kill. Fix the patch and
re-run; do not record it as a surviving mutation.
This ledger is NOT written back to by the runner. Every record here is a claim the runner
re-checks from scratch, so an archived `observed` string would be a second copy of an
answer the run already produces -- and a second copy is a second thing that can rot.

kills.reproduces the paper's printed A^⊗2: the paper's own published power no longer matches
kills.both parties compute the brief’s shared: the worked instance's key changes entirely

product-takes-max.why: Max-plus instead of min-plus. This is the single substitution the whole platform is, so the paper's printed vectors are the right thing to catch it.

kills.U, V and the shared key are the brief’s: instance C's U, V and K all change when the constant term is dropped
kills.includes the constant term, as the paper: the one-cell case that isolates the decision

polynomial-drops-constant-term.why: The paper's sums run from i = 0. This is recorded against acceptance check C on purpose: check B's U and K do NOT change when the constant term is dropped, so an implementation verified only against B would pass this mutation. One worked example cannot settle this question, which is why there are two.

kills.the recovered key equals the honest key,: the recovered key comes out short by c in every entry

heuristic-forgets-the-constant.why: X = c ⊗ A^⊗i, not A^⊗i. Without the scalar, X ⊗ Y differs from U by exactly c in every cell and the recovered key is off by c everywhere -- a result that looks entirely well-formed and is wrong. On the worked instance c = 3.

kills.X ⊗ Y equals U: without the inequalities the solver returns x, y whose product is not U
kills.solves the system: invariant 3 rejects the result rather than reporting it

general-attack-skips-the-inequalities.why: Enforces the cover's equalities and drops the constraint that every other term sits at or above zero. The system is then under-constrained and the solution it returns does not reproduce U -- which invariant 3's X ⊗ Y = U check is there to catch before any key is shown.

kills.both parties compute the brief’s shared: Bob's key stops matching Alice's and the brief's
kills.both parties agree on a fresh designers: the agreement property fails on random instances too

bob-folds-his-own-message.why: Each party folds the OTHER party's message. Folding his own gives Bob q1(A) ⊗ V ⊗ q2(B), which is not the shared key -- and `keysAgree` is computed from a real comparison, so the page's verdict follows.

recovered-means-returned-something.find: return { recovered: mismatches.length === 0, conditions, candidateKey, mismatches };
recovered-means-returned-something.replace: return { recovered: candidateKey !== null, conditions, candidateKey, mismatches };

kills.negative claim bite: a well-formed key t: the fixture where the attack returns a well-formed matrix that is not the key

recovered-means-returned-something.why: Invariant 1, inverted: the verdict becomes 'the attack returned a matrix' instead of 'the recovered key equals the honest key'. Only the wrong-message fixture separates the two -- on every ordinary instance the attack's answer IS the key, so this mutation is invisible without it. That fixture is why the negative claim is testable rather than a disclaimer.

kills.refuses a commuting pair inside runExcha: and runExchange stops refusing with it

commuting-pair-accepted.why: Invariant 4. With commuting bases every message is a polynomial in one commutative algebra and the exchange carries no secret at all -- so this has to fail closed rather than quietly producing a key.

kills.finds the brief’s (i, j, c) — i = 2, j =: the only constant difference sits at j = 3, so the scan finds nothing
kills.(2, 3) is the ONLY constant difference i: the measurement that makes the above a kill rather than a coincidence

scan-stops-one-short.why: An off-by-one in the scan's upper bound. Recorded against the j loop specifically: on the worked instance the only constant difference is at i = 2, j = 3, so bounding i at D-1 leaves it reachable and kills nothing. Which bound is mutated is part of the patch, not a detail.

comment: The a11y oracles were mutation-checked the same way on 2026-11-15, by hand rather than
through this runner -- they judge RENDERED PIXELS, so the patch is a CSS token and the
oracle is a Playwright project rather than a named unit test. Recorded here so the result
is replayable:
--control-border #7d756a -> #39312a : the non-text oracle reported NEW 1.48:1 (needs
3:1) [control-boundary] on button.btn.btn-ghost.cell-btn, naming the token, the
measured ratio and the threshold. Restored; the oracle went quiet again.
--text-dim #b8b0a4 -> #6b635a : axe's own color-contrast rule failed the arrival state.
.verdict-pass gains color: #5c564e : failed naming .verdict-text inside two specific
data-verdict markers.
A capture run (NT_BASELINE_CAPTURE=1) over the whole drive prints zero findings, which is
why e2e/nontext-baseline.ts is empty -- the terminal state of the ratchet, not an unrun
check. The three mutations above are what separate those two readings.
